baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Households placed on the urban lot: linked parish, census and tax records for nineteenth-century Montreal, mapped with GIS at McGill in the 1990s and built from 2000 into the collective MAP geodatabase
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (Atlas historique du Québec, 1997; read in full) works from 'l’exemple local pour ensuite faire ressortir la vue d’ensemble et saisir ainsi, dans une démarche exploratoire, les processus par lesquels la cité se construit' (p. 81). Its samples are built from records, and differ by population: the Catholic baptismal cohort of 1859, whose parents were traced through the Drouin index and the Notre-Dame registers (n. 4); for the Protestant population only, a micro-sample of ten surnames ('Pour la population protestante, notre microéchantillon s’appuie sur dix patronymes', p. 85), distinct from the twelve-surname sampling that the publisher's description gives for the later book with Thornton (2011, unread here); a 'Montréal « miniaturisé »' of 370 household heads in 1900, and building tradesmen from the 'rôle d’évaluation' plotted in half-kilometre rings 'à la manière d’une reconstitution cinématographique' (p. 89). Note 1 credits the demographic analysis to Patricia Thornton and the mapping 'sur ATLAS GIS' to Ben Johnson and Ingrid Olson, with the McGill GIS laboratory. Earlier work is known only at title level ('Occupations and Residential Spaces', Historical Methods, 1989) or from an abstract (with Gilliland, Urban History Review, 1998: 'From small samples of the Montreal population over the years 1861-1901'). After 2000, her own words. In 2004 she describes the method and its limits: cross-referencing the 1842 census, the 1848 directory and the 1848 taxroll 'in an iterative process of matching surnames, first names, streets of residence, and occupations'; of 5,192 taxroll entries '75 per cent can be matched to the directory, 45 per cent to the census 5 years earlier, and 41 per cent to both sources' (Labour/Le Travail 53, pp. 173–74). In the same note Robert Sweeny 'has created from the Cane map an electronic framework' (p. 165, note). With Dufaux (2014): MAP is 'a collective project in which dozens of people have invested their skills'; 'The spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot – 7,000 lots in the 1850s, 30,000 in 1900' (p. 155); 'A dozen Montreal scholars and a dozen graduate students initiated the project in 2000' (p. 176 n. 1). From abstracts: the 2010 and 2011 papers with Gilliland (and Gauvreau) locate '17,000 individual households' in 1881 and re-aggregate lots into 'districts with identical boundaries for both years', 'overcoming the major methodological problems hindering previous comparative analyses'. Reception (later readings, labelled). Bonnell and Fortin (2014, p. xii): 'Since the 1990s, only a small number of historical geographers and historians have used GIS technology' in Canada; 'Notable projects include Montréal, l’avenir du passé, a comprehensive HGIS database of Montreal led by McGill geographer Sherry Olson and Memorial University historian Robert Sweeny'; 'Olson, Sweeny, and Gilliland’s work has captured the interest of a new generation of graduate students and new scholars' (p. xiii). Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014, p. 11): 'we are following the lead of Sherry Olson, whose pioneering work on nineteenth-century Montreal is a model of spatial history'; their n. 31 lists her 'foundational studies'. That chapter is not independent: Gilliland was her MAP collaborator. Contested: Sweeny, MAP's co-director (Digital Studies, 2009), argues that 'The ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding', that a GIS ensures 'the illusion of accuracy', and that 'an historical GIS works because it is a-historical'. This is a critique of the instrument from inside the project, not of Olson. Not a founding: the editors give the US and British national repositories as 'some of the most important work in the field' (p. xi), and the strand's Gregory and Southall (1998) is a separate, aggregate-boundary tradition. 'Pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, not this entry's.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: City building in long swings: Baltimore's growth read through cycles of investment, construction and neighbourhood change (1979–80), and Montreal's through its builders and migrants (1997–2011)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. Baltimore (1980; introduction and acknowledgments read): 'There is a tempo and a pattern to urban growth'; 'City growth is a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks. This applies equally to North America and Europe over at least two centuries'; 'This book is about city building, an internal dynamic of the city-state, and how Baltimoreans see themselves and their situation. In that sense, Baltimore is America, in its rhythm of building up and tearing down, swarming and dispersing' (pp. ix–x). She names what the book leaves out: 'The most serious gap is our ignorance of the lives of slaves and servants in Baltimore', the Polish Catholic community, and 'the strategies of landowners and real estate investors in each round' (pp. ix–x). The acknowledgments record that 'David Harvey shared his discovery of Baltimore for several years' (p. vii). The 1979 Annals article (abstract only): 'The long-swing rhythm of urban investment has produced distinctive spaces and forms in the city', with 'a tempo and a spatial matrix for income redistribution, social conflict, and social pathology'. Montreal (1997, read in full): migration 'Récurrentes de 20 ans en 20 ans' (p. 81); half the population lived within a kilometre of the centre in 1861, in the next ring by 1881 and the one beyond by 1901, as the building trades, 'telle une vague déferlante, se déplacent vers la périphérie' (p. 89). Reception. In-period reviews of Baltimore appeared in the AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture and JEH (1981) and in JIH and the Journal of Historical Geography (1982); none could be read here (JSTOR, OUP and Elsevier walls; the JEH first-page preview image was illegible), so no in-period judgement is reported. Later readings, snippet witnesses (opening paragraphs only): Sager (CHR, 2012) reads Peopling the North American City (2011, unread here) as 'an example of the research collaboratory that has emerged in recent decades'; Horner (HS/SH, 2013) says it 'makes a vital contribution not only to the historiography of Montreal and Quebec, but also to the way that historians and geographers conceptualize the relationship between individuals, families, communities and urban space'. A contribution to the field's building-and-space strand beside Warner, not a new school.
